claim: Exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells can initiate malignant cell transformation.
source: To understand how exosomes might contribute to cell transformation, we utilized the classic two-step NIH/3T3 cell transformation assay and observed that exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells, but not normal human cells, can initiate malignant cell transformation and these transformed cells formed tumors in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, supported by experimental results from the two-step cell transformation assay and in vivo tumor formation studies shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Exosomes isolated from normal human cells cannot initiate malignant cell transformation.
source: To understand how exosomes might contribute to cell transformation, we utilized the classic two-step NIH/3T3 cell transformation assay and observed that exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells, but not normal human cells, can initiate malignant cell transformation and these transformed cells formed tumors in vivo.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that HPDE cell exosomes and primary fibroblast exosomes did not result in increased cell transformation.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes are unable to transform cells alone.
source: However, cancer cell exosomes are unable to transform cells alone or to act as a promoter of cell transformation.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that treatment with exosomes alone resulted in only background levels of foci formation.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes are unable to act as a promoter of cell transformation.
source: However, cancer cell exosomes are unable to transform cells alone or to act as a promoter of cell transformation.
evidence: The abstract states this directly, supported by experimental data in Figure 2C showing that MCA/exosome treatment resulted in only background levels of foci formation.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes act as an initiator by inducing random mutations in recipient cells.
source: Utilizing proteomics and exome sequencing, we discovered cancer cell exosomes act as an initiator by inducing random mutations in recipient cells.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by exome sequencing data presented in Figures 5 and 6 showing diverse mutational profiles in transformed foci.

claim: Cells from the pool of randomly mutated cells are driven to transformation by a classic promoter resulting in foci, each of which encode a unique genetic profile.
source: Cells from the pool of randomly mutated cells are driven to transformation by a classic promoter resulting in foci, each of which encode a unique genetic profile.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by exome sequencing data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing unique variants in each foci.

claim: Transformed cells formed from cancer cell exosome initiation formed tumors in vivo.
source: To understand how exosomes might contribute to cell transformation, we utilized the classic two-step NIH/3T3 cell transformation assay and observed that exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells, but not normal human cells, can initiate malignant cell transformation and these transformed cells formed tumors in vivo.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by in vivo tumor formation data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Exosomes are small (30–150 nm) secreted extracellular vesicles shed by normal and malignant cells.
source: The conversation at the primary tumor site, as well as at distant locations, is mediated through many secreted factors including exosomes; small (30–150 nm) secreted extracellular vesicles shed by normal and malignant cells (Kalluri, 2016; Costa-Silva et al., 2015; Stahl and Raposo, 2018; Colombo et al., 2014; Willms et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of exosomes supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Exosomes carry heterogeneous cargo composed of proteins, metabolites, genetic material (DNA and microRNAs), and lipids.
source: Based on multi-omic studies, exosomes are known to carry heterogeneous cargo composed of proteins, metabolites, genetic material (DNA and microRNAs), and lipids (Willms et al., 2016; Demory Beckler et al., 2013; Kowal et al., 2016; Kalluri and LeBleu, 2016; Melo et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about exosome composition supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Exosomes are crucial in shaping the local tumor microenvironment to promote cancer progression by advancing tumor metastasis.
source: A growing body of evidence shows exosomes are crucial in shaping the local tumor microenvironment to promote cancer progression by advancing tumor metastasis (Costa-Silva et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature demonstrating the role of exosomes in metastasis.

claim: Mutations in the four pancreatic driver genes, KRAS, CDKN2A, TP53, and SMAD4, occur frequently in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC).
source: Mutations in the four pancreatic driver genes, KRAS, CDKN2A, TP53, and SMAD4, occur frequently in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas (PDAC) and are well described (Giovannetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDAC genetics supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: An activating mutation in the KRAS gene is present in 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cases.
source: An activating mutation in the KRAS gene is present in 90% of cases (Giovannetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KRAS mutations in PDAC supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Capan-2, MIA PaCa-2, and Panc-1 pancreatic cancer cell lines have oncogenic mutations in the KRAS gene.
source: Of note, three of the cancer cell lines, Capan-2, MIA PaCa-2, and Panc-1, have oncogenic mutations in the KRAS gene, whereas BxPC-3 has wild-type KRAS (Deer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by citation to prior literature characterizing these cell lines.

claim: BxPC-3 pancreatic cancer cell line has wild-type KRAS.
source: Of note, three of the cancer cell lines, Capan-2, MIA PaCa-2, and Panc-1, have oncogenic mutations in the KRAS gene, whereas BxPC-3 has wild-type KRAS (Deer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by citation to prior literature characterizing this cell line.

claim: Capan-2 exosomes contain common exosomal marker proteins CD63, Alix, and TSG101.
source: Immunoblot analysis was used to confirm the presence of expected exosomal marker proteins (CD63, Alix, and TSG101) as well as the absence of proteins not commonly found in exosomes (Calnexin, α-actinin, and HSP90) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Capan-2 exosomes lack proteins Calnexin, α-actinin, and HSP90.
source: Immunoblot analysis was used to confirm the presence of expected exosomal marker proteins (CD63, Alix, and TSG101) as well as the absence of proteins not commonly found in exosomes (Calnexin, α-actinin, and HSP90) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Capan-2 exosomes contain the top twenty most commonly found proteins in exosomes according to the ExoCarta database.
source: In addition to western blot analysis, mass spectrometry analysis of isolated exosomes confirms the presence of the top twenty most commonly found proteins in exosomes according to the ExoCarta database (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) (Keerthikumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Capan-2 exosomes show round or cup-shaped morphology by TEM.
source: TEM images of exosomes isolated from Capan-2 cells show the expected round or cup-shaped morphology (Willms et al., 2016) and NTA shows the size distribution of exosomes centered on 91 nm with a mean size of 250.3 nm (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by TEM images shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Capan-2 exosomes have a size distribution centered on 91 nm with a mean size of 250.3 nm.
source: TEM images of exosomes isolated from Capan-2 cells show the expected round or cup-shaped morphology (Willms et al., 2016) and NTA shows the size distribution of exosomes centered on 91 nm with a mean size of 250.3 nm (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by nanoparticle tracking analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with both MCA as the initiator and TPA as the promoter resulted in formation of 3–4 foci/well on average.
source: By contrast, cells treated with both MCA as the initiator and TPA as the promoter resulted in formation of 3–4 foci/well on average (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cells that are untreated, treated with only an initiator (MCA), or only a promoter (TPA) show the formation of low levels of background foci (one foci/well on average).
source: Cells that are untreated, treated with only an initiator (MCA), or only a promoter (TPA) show the formation of low levels of background foci (one foci/well on average) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1) (Sasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells treated with Capan-2 exosomes as an initiator and TPA as a promoter resulted in increased cell transformation.
source: However, when the cancer cell exosomes were tested as an initiator in combination with the promoter TPA, cell transformation was observed at similar levels as the chemical MCA/TPA treatment (3–4 foci/well) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells treated with MIA PaCa-2 exosomes as an initiator and TPA as a promoter resulted in increased cell transformation.
source: However, when the cancer cell exosomes were tested as an initiator in combination with the promoter TPA, cell transformation was observed at similar levels as the chemical MCA/TPA treatment (3–4 foci/well) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells treated with Panc-1 exosomes as an initiator and TPA as a promoter resulted in increased cell transformation.
source: However, when the cancer cell exosomes were tested as an initiator in combination with the promoter TPA, cell transformation was observed at similar levels as the chemical MCA/TPA treatment (3–4 foci/well) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes isolated from three different pancreatic cancer cell lines can each function as an initiator in the CTA resulting in transformation of NIH/3T3 cells.
source: Therefore, exosomes derived from three different pancreatic cancer cell lines (Capan-2, MIA PaCa-2 or Panc-1) can each function as an initiator in the CTA resulting in transformation of NIH/3T3 cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes isolated from WT KRAS BxPC-3 cells can act as an initiator of cell transformation.
source: We observed that cancer cell exosomes isolated from WT KRAS BxPC-3 cells can act as an initiator of cell transformation, resulting in foci formation similar to the numbers observed with MCA/TPA treatment (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Normal cell exosomes isolated from HPDE cells were unable to induce cell transformation when used as an initiator in the CTA.
source: However, normal cell exosomes isolated from HPDE cells or exosomes from primary fibroblasts were unable to induce cell transformation when used as an initiator in the CTA (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Exosomes from primary fibroblasts were unable to induce cell transformation when used as an initiator in the CTA.
source: However, normal cell exosomes isolated from HPDE cells or exosomes from primary fibroblasts were unable to induce cell transformation when used as an initiator in the CTA (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pancreatic cancer cell exosomes can act as an initiator in malignant cell transformation of NIH/3T3 cells, while exosomes isolated from normal pancreatic cells or primary fibroblasts cannot.
source: Collectively, the results show that pancreatic cancer cell exosomes can act as an initiator in malignant cell transformation of NIH/3T3 cells, while exosomes isolated from normal pancreatic cells or primary fibroblasts cannot.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Purified exosomes (Fraction 3) from Capan-2 cells have a size range centered on 67 nm with a mean size of 83.5 nm.
source: Characterization of these purified exosomes (Fraction 3) by NTA showed a size range centered on 67 nm with a mean size of 83.5 nm.
evidence: This is demonstrated by nanoparticle tracking analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Purified exosomes (Fraction 3) from Capan-2 cells contain expected exosomal marker proteins CD63 and Alix.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed the presence of expected exosomal marker proteins CD63 and Alix.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Purified exosomes retain the ability to act as an initiator of cell transformation.
source: The purified exosomes were then tested as an initiator with the promoter TPA in the transformation assay and results show that the population of 'pure' exosomes retain the ability to act as an initiator of cell transformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Initiator activity of cancer cell exosomes requires one dose of exosomes over a 3-day period with a protein concentration of at least 8 ng/mL.
source: This indicates that initiator activity of cancer cell exosomes requires one dose of exosomes over a 3-day period with a protein concentration of at least 8 ng/mL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response studies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: When cancer cell exosomes are boiled for 10 min at 100°C just prior to use as an initiator, the level of transformed foci decreases to background levels.
source: Furthermore, when cancer cell exosomes are boiled for 10 min at 100°C just prior to use as an initiator, the level of transformed foci decreases to background levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells treated with either MCA or Capan-2 exosomes as the initiator followed by treatment with CdCl2 as the promoter resulted in formation of foci similar to that observed with TPA as the promoter.
source: We observed that NIH/3T3 cells treated with either MCA or Capan-2 exosomes as the initiator followed by treatment with CdCl2 as the promoter resulted in formation of foci similar to that observed with TPA as the promoter (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment of cells with CdCl2 alone resulted in background levels of foci.
source: Treatment of cells with CdCl2 alone resulted in background levels of foci, reiterating the fact that cell transformation is dependent on both initiation and promotion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells act as general initiators in the transformation assay and are not dependent on a specific promoter.
source: These results indicate that exosomes isolated from pancreatic cancer cells act as general initiators in the transformation assay and are not dependent on a specific promoter.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data showing that cancer cell exosomes work with both TPA and CdCl2 as promoters (Figure 2D).

claim: Tumor growth was observed in mice injected with cells from the chemically treated MCA/TPA foci at all three concentrations tested.
source: After 37 days, tumor growth was observed in mice injected with cells from the chemically treated MCA/TPA foci and the cancer cell (Capan-2) exosome/TPA treated foci, at all three concentrations tested, whereas no tumor growth was observed in any of the mice injected with non-transformed control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in mice injected with cells from the cancer cell (Capan-2) exosome/TPA treated foci at all three concentrations tested.
source: After 37 days, tumor growth was observed in mice injected with cells from the chemically treated MCA/TPA foci and the cancer cell (Capan-2) exosome/TPA treated foci, at all three concentrations tested, whereas no tumor growth was observed in any of the mice injected with non-transformed control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: No tumor growth was observed in any of the mice injected with non-transformed control cells.
source: After 37 days, tumor growth was observed in mice injected with cells from the chemically treated MCA/TPA foci and the cancer cell (Capan-2) exosome/TPA treated foci, at all three concentrations tested, whereas no tumor growth was observed in any of the mice injected with non-transformed control cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Higher concentrations of cells resulted in faster growth and larger tumors.
source: In each case, the appearance of the tumors formed correlated with the number of cells injected, as higher concentrations of cells resulted in faster growth and larger tumors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Histological analysis confirmed that the tumors are fibrosarcomas.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that the tumors are fibrosarcomas, as was expected because cells used in the CTA are NIH/3T3 cells from a mesenchymal origin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by histological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cells collected from MIA PaCa-2 exosome/TPA, Panc-1 exosome/TPA, and BxPC-3 exosome/TPA foci formed tumors in mice at varying size and growth rates.
source: Using a concentration of 1 × 106 cells, we observed that cells collected from MIA PaCa-2 exosome/TPA, Panc-1 exosome/TPA, and BxPC-3 exosome/TPA foci formed tumors in mice at varying size and growth rates (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: After injection of untreated background foci, 6 out of 15 total mice formed tumors.
source: After injection of untreated background foci, we observed that 6 out of 15 total mice formed tumors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Tumors from untreated background foci grew later in the time course and at a significantly slower rate compared to initiator and promoter treated transformed foci cells.
source: Notably, each of the six tumors (five from the same injected foci) grew later in the time course and at a significantly slower rate compared to initiator and promoter treated transformed foci cells, as has been previously observed (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) (Xu and Rubin, 1990).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, and supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No marked global changes in protein content were observed for cells treated with MCA or Capan-2 exosomes when compared to proteins found in untreated NIH/3T3 cells.
source: No marked global changes in protein content were observed for cells treated with MCA (yellow) or Capan-2 exosomes (blue) when compared to proteins found in untreated NIH/3T3 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by proteomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 'common' proteins found in both the untreated control and the transformed foci showed a high degree of overlap between foci of the same type.
source: The 'common' proteins found in both the untreated control and the transformed foci were compared using Venn diagrams and showed a high degree of overlap between foci of the same type (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The proteins found to be 'unique' to each foci and absent in the control cells showed very little overlap between foci of the same type.
source: By contrast, the proteins found to be 'unique' to each foci and absent in the control cells were compared and showed very little overlap between foci of the same type (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When all 12 foci samples were plotted together, the six transformed foci (MCA/TPA and Capan-2/TPA) appeared to cluster tightly while the six background foci (untreated and TPA-only) showed no clear relationship to one another.
source: When all 12 foci samples were plotted together, the six transformed foci (MCA/TPA and Capan-2/TPA) appeared to cluster tightly while the six background foci (untreated and TPA-only) showed no clear relationship to one another (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PCA of just the six transformed foci showed that there is no clear relationship between these samples.
source: When probed further, PCA of just the six transformed foci showed that there is no clear relationship between these samples (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Clustering analysis of mutational signatures shows that all six transformed foci have similar mutational profiles that vary from the six background foci samples.
source: Clustering analysis of these signatures shows that all six transformed foci have similar mutational profiles that vary from the six background foci samples.
evidence: This is demonstrated by clustering analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The top mutational signatures found in each of the six transformed foci are COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15.
source: The top mutational signatures found in each of the six transformed foci are COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15 (Figure 6), both of which are associated with defective DNA mismatch repair (MMR) and microsatellite instability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MutaGene analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15 are associated with defective DNA mismatch repair (MMR) and microsatellite instability.
source: The top mutational signatures found in each of the six transformed foci are COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15 (Figure 6), both of which are associated with defective DNA mismatch repair (MMR) and microsatellite instability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COSMIC mutational signatures.

claim: The top COSMIC Signature associated with each of the background foci was found to be COSMIC Signature 3, associated with failure of DNA double-strand break-repair.
source: Instead, the top COSMIC Signature associated with each of the background foci was found to be COSMIC Signature 3, associated with failure of DNA double-strand break-repair.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MutaGene analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Missense mutations were found in mismatch repair genes in each of the transformed foci.
source: Missense mutations were found to be encoded in each of the transformed foci, but none of the foci contained the same mutations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MMR gene mutations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the transformed foci contained the same mutations in mismatch repair genes.
source: Missense mutations were found to be encoded in each of the transformed foci, but none of the foci contained the same mutations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MMR gene mutations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: None of the untreated background foci had mutations in the analyzed MMR genes.
source: None of the untreated background foci and only one of the TPA-only treated background foci had mutations in the analyzed MMR genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MMR gene mutations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only one of the TPA-only treated background foci had mutations in the analyzed MMR genes.
source: None of the untreated background foci and only one of the TPA-only treated background foci had mutations in the analyzed MMR genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of MMR gene mutations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Very few shared mutations were observed between independent foci of the same type in oncogenes.
source: Results did not indicate a likely driver mutation as very few shared mutations were observed between independent foci of the same type and no common point mutations were found (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of oncogene mutations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No common point mutations were found in oncogenes across the 12 foci samples.
source: Results did not indicate a likely driver mutation as very few shared mutations were observed between independent foci of the same type and no common point mutations were found (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of oncogene mutations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A single treatment of cancer cell exosomes on NIH/3T3 cells over 3 days can act in a similar way as the chemical initiator MCA, by randomly incorporating molecular changes into DNA.
source: We propose that a single treatment of cancer cell exosomes on NIH/3T3 cells over 3 days can act in a similar way as the chemical initiator MCA, by randomly incorporating molecular changes into DNA.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data showing similar transformation outcomes and mutational profiles.

claim: MCA creates an identifiable tumor phenotype long before the appearance of tumors and causes changes in DNA structure that could be expected to influence gene expression and further translation.
source: According to Malins et al., MCA creates an identifiable tumor phenotype long before the appearance of tumors and causes changes in DNA structure that could be expected to influence gene expression and further translation (Malins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCA mechanism supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: MCA is known to produce bulky carcinogen-DNA adducts, which are associated with G·C → T·A transversions.
source: The biochemistry associated with MCA-driven transformation is complex and diverse; it is known to produce bulky carcinogen-DNA adducts, which are associated with G·C → T·A transversions and thus introduces mutagenic and carcinogenic properties into DNA (Malins et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MCA mechanism supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Exosomes do not uniformly contain the same pool of proteins, lipids, metabolites, or microRNAs, but rather each exosome contains a unique repertoire of biological molecules.
source: Additionally, it is known that exosomes do not uniformly contain the same pool of proteins, lipids, metabolites, or microRNAs, but rather each exosome contains a unique repertoire of biological molecules thus possibly causing a variety of changes in the cells (Willms et al., 2016; Kowal et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about exosome heterogeneity supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Analysis of the top signatures for all six transformed foci shows that mutations in mismatch repair machinery are most likely what drives the transformation of these cells.
source: Analysis of the top signatures for all six transformed foci shows that mutations in mismatch repair machinery are most likely what drives the transformation of these cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MutaGene analysis showing COSMIC Signatures 20 and 15 as top contributors in transformed foci.

claim: When TPA is used as a promoter in combination with a functional initiator, the molecular path of cells towards tumorigenesis may not be random.
source: These observations support the proposal that when TPA is used as a promoter (to drive proliferation) in combination with a functional initiator (an entity that creates a population of randomly mutated cells), the molecular path of cells towards tumorigenesis may not be random.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observation that all transformed foci share similar mutational signatures despite originating from random mutations.

claim: TPA may drive a path in a subset of randomly mutated cells that accommodates a course towards COSMIC signatures 20 or 15.
source: Rather, TPA may drive a path in a subset of randomly mutated cells that accommodates a course towards COSMIC signatures 20 or 15.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observation that all transformed foci share similar mutational signatures.

claim: A portion of co-occurring IPMNs in PDAC patients appeared to be genetically unrelated, meaning they shared no mutations in the assayed genes.
source: A recent study by Felsentein et al. described an interesting finding in which a portion of co-occurring IPMNs in PDAC patients appeared to be genetically unrelated, meaning they shared no mutations in the assayed genes (Felsenstein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Cells in a primary tumor could be derived from independent transformation events as opposed to exclusive clonal events.
source: This elicits a fascinating question as to whether cells in a primary tumor could be derived from independent transformation events as opposed to exclusive clonal events (Felsenstein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative question raised based on findings from prior literature.

claim: Exosomes secreted by the primary tumor could orchestrate independent transformation events.
source: This elicits a fascinating question as to whether cells in a primary tumor could be derived from independent transformation events as opposed to exclusive clonal events (Felsenstein et al., 2018). Potentially, exosomes secreted by the primary tumor could orchestrate such events.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings that cancer cell exosomes can initiate transformation.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes have the capacity to act as a classic initiator in the 2-stage CTA by incorporating random changes to NIH/3T3 cells over three days to mediate the first step in cell transformation.
source: In conclusion, we observe that cancer cell exosomes have the capacity to act as a classic initiator in the 2-stage CTA by incorporating random changes to NIH/3T3 cells over three days to mediate the first step in cell transformation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all experimental data presented.

claim: Exosomes from pancreatic cancer cell lines, independently from the KRAS mutation status, can initiate the transformation of NIH/3T3 cells.
source: We observe that exosomes from pancreatic cancer cell lines, independently from the KRAS mutation status, can initiate the transformation of NIH/3T3 cells, while exosomes from normal pancreatic cells do not possess this ability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing that both KRAS mutant and wild-type cancer cell exosomes can initiate transformation.

claim: Exosomes from normal pancreatic cells do not possess the ability to initiate transformation of NIH/3T3 cells.
source: We observe that exosomes from pancreatic cancer cell lines, independently from the KRAS mutation status, can initiate the transformation of NIH/3T3 cells, while exosomes from normal pancreatic cells do not possess this ability.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing that HPDE cell exosomes cannot initiate transformation.

claim: The classic two-stage CTA is a tiered system for transformation that was created for screening potential carcinogenic factors.
source: The classic two-stage in vitro cell transformation assay (CTA) is a tiered system for transformation that was created for screening potential carcinogenic factors (Berwald and SACHS, 1963; Kakunaga, 1973; Sakai and Sato, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CTA supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the two-stage CTA, cells are first treated with a suspected carcinogen, called an initiator, such as the genotoxic carcinogen 3-MCA.
source: In this system, cells are first treated with a suspected carcinogen, called an initiator, such as the genotoxic carcinogen 3-MCA (3-methylcholanthrene).
evidence: This is a description of the standard CTA protocol supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 3-MCA introduces random genetic changes in a pool of normal cells.
source: 3-MCA introduces random genetic changes in a pool of normal cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of MCA as an initiator.

claim: Initiated cells are exposed to a promoter, such as TPA, which enhances proliferation in the initiated cells selectively, thus driving malignant transformation of the cells.
source: Subsequently, these initiated cells are exposed to a promoter, such as TPA (12-O-tetradecanoylphorbol 13-acetate), which enhances proliferation in the initiated cells selectively, thus driving malignant transformation of the cells.
evidence: This is a description of the standard CTA protocol and mechanism.

claim: The resulting transformed cells are observed as foci on a cell culture plate.
source: The resulting transformed cells are observed as foci on a cell culture plate (Sakai and Sato, 1989; Sasaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the standard CTA readout supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The CTA provides sensitivity in detecting a wider range of initiating agents that may not show obvious transforming activity without a promoter.
source: This reductionist approach provides sensitivity in detecting a wider range of initiating agents that may not show obvious transforming activity without a promoter (Sakai and Sato, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the advantages of the CTA supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Exosomes can contribute to the transformation of nontumorigenic cells to form tumors.
source: It has been shown that exosomes can contribute to the transformation of nontumorigenic cells to form tumors (Melo et al., 2014; Dai et al., 2018; Abdouh et al., 2017; Hamam et al., 2016; Antonyak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by multiple citations.

claim: In previous studies showing exosome-mediated transformation, cells were either pre-exposed to transforming agents or treated with cancer patient sera or medium from cultured cancer cells, both of which contain cancer cell exosomes.
source: However, a common feature among these studies is the use of cells that were either pre-exposed to transforming agents or treated with cancer patient sera or medium from cultured cancer cells, both of which contain cancer cell exosomes.
evidence: This is an observation about the design of prior studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Under conditions where cells are pre-exposed to transforming agents or treated with cancer patient sera, it is conceivable that other components, in addition to exosomes, are transforming cells.
source: Under these conditions, it is conceivable that other components, in addition to exosomes, are transforming cells.
evidence: This is a logical inference about potential confounding factors in prior studies.

claim: Pancreatic cancer is a lethal metastatic disease that lacks efficient curative treatment.
source: Pancreatic cancer is a lethal metastatic disease that lacks efficient curative treatment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about pancreatic cancer.

claim: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths in the world.
source: Even though there is continuing progress toward understanding the biology of pancreatic cancer, it remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths in the world (Vincent et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pancreatic cancer supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The lack of effective treatments against pancreatic cancer's highly metastatic behavior is the main reason it remains a leading cause of cancer-related deaths.
source: This is mainly due to the lack of effective treatments against its highly metastatic behavior and therefore, understanding the key mechanisms underlying its progression is needed.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the challenges in treating pancreatic cancer.

claim: Genetic heterogeneity and polyclonality have been shown to be present in PDAC.
source: Additionally, genetic heterogeneity and polyclonality have also been shown to be present in PDAC (Giovannetti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PDAC genetics supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Malignant transformation of a normal cell occurs in a stepwise fashion.
source: Malignant transformation of a normal cell occurs in a stepwise fashion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the process of cell transformation.

claim: Point mutations in the genome can result in the reprogramming of a normal cell to a less differentiated state that is receptive to additional genetic alterations resulting in uncontrolled growth and ultimately cancer.
source: Point mutations in the genome can result in the reprogramming of a normal cell to a less differentiated state that is receptive to additional genetic alterations resulting in uncontrolled growth and ultimately cancer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of cell transformation.

claim: Treatment with both an initiator and promoter was required to observe increased cell transformation as evidenced by formation of an increased number of foci above background levels.
source: Consistent with previous findings, treatment with both an initiator and promoter was required to observe increased cell transformation as evidenced by formation of an increased number of foci above background levels (Sakai and Sato, 1989).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data in Figure 2C and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells treated with cancer cell exosomes for the duration of the initiation and promotion steps resulted in the formation of only background transformation activity.
source: NIH/3T3 cells were first treated with isolated exosomes from each of the three pancreatic cancer cell lines for the duration of the initiation and promotion steps (3-week treatment). This resulted in the formation of only background transformation activity, similar to what is observed with the untreated control (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: NIH/3T3 cells treated with the initiator MCA and then subsequently treated with isolated cancer cell exosomes for the 2-week promotion period resulted in only background levels of foci.
source: Next, NIH/3T3 cells were first treated with the initiator MCA and then subsequently treated with isolated cancer cell exosomes for the 2-week promotion period. For each of these three cancer cell exosome assays, again only background levels of foci were observed (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The initiator activity of pancreatic cancer cell exosomes is a trait unique to exosomes derived from cancer cells and not a general characteristic of exosomes from all cell types.
source: To assess whether this initiator activity is a general characteristic of exosomes from all cell types or a trait unique to exosomes derived from KRAS mutated pancreatic cancer cell lines, we repeated experiments with exosomes from three additional cell types: BxPC-3 cells, a pancreatic cancer cell line with WT KRAS, HPDE cells, a normal human cell line, and primary dermal fibroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental design and results showing that only cancer cell exosomes, not normal cell exosomes, can initiate transformation.

claim: The ultrafiltration-ultracentrifugation method used for exosome isolation is known to result in a preparation containing both exosomes and aggregated protein/nucleic acid contaminants.
source: Our results demonstrate a specific function for cancer cell exosomes, but we used a protocol that is known to result in a preparation containing both exosomes and aggregated protein/nucleic acid contaminants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the limitations of the ultrafiltration-ultracentrifugation method.

claim: Floating exosomes onto a sucrose density gradient obtains cleaner exosome preparation separated from contaminants.
source: For this reason, we performed an additional purification step by floating exosomes onto a sucrose density gradient to obtain cleaner exosome preparation separated from contaminants (Chiou and Ansel, 2016).
evidence: This is an established method for exosome purification supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: A standard concentration of 80 ng/mL of proteins (corresponding to 7.0 × 107 particles/mL) was used in each transformation assay.
source: As a standard concentration in each transformation assay, we used 80 ng/mL of proteins, corresponding to 7.0 × 107 particles/mL.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as the standard concentration used in experiments.

claim: Equal cell transformation was observed for all exosome concentrations tested except the two lowest, 0.08 ng/mL and 0.8 ng/mL.
source: Exosome protein concentrations ranging from 0.08 ng/mL to 2400 ng/mL were tested and we observed equal cell transformation for all concentrations with the exception of the two lowest, 0.08 ng/mL and 0.8 ng/mL.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response studies shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Intact exosomes are required for initiator activity.
source: Furthermore, when cancer cell exosomes are boiled for 10 min at 100°C just prior to use as an initiator, the level of transformed foci decreases to background levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that boiling exosomes (which destroys membrane structures) eliminates initiator activity.

claim: Boiling exosomes destroys the membrane structures and releases the vesicle content into the media.
source: Boiling exosomes destroys the membrane structures and releases the vesicle content into the media, demonstrating that intact vesicles are needed to induce cell transformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effect of boiling on exosome structure.

claim: Intact vesicles are needed to induce cell transformation.
source: Boiling exosomes destroys the membrane structures and releases the vesicle content into the media, demonstrating that intact vesicles are needed to induce cell transformation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that boiled exosomes lose initiator activity.

claim: One common characteristic of initiators in the CTA is the capability of working with multiple promoters to induce cell transformation.
source: One common characteristic of initiators in the CTA is the capability of working with multiple promoters to induce cell transformation (Fang et al., 2001; Sakai, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about initiators in the CTA supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell transformation is dependent on both initiation and promotion.
source: Treatment of cells with CdCl2 alone resulted in background levels of foci, reiterating the fact that cell transformation is dependent on both initiation and promotion.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing that CdCl2 alone does not induce transformation.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in all mice injected with MCA/TPA transformed cells at a concentration of 1 × 106 cells.
source: Additional in vivo experiments include subcutaneous injection of mice (n = 5/group) with 1 × 106 cells isolated after treatment with MIA PaCa-2 (ExM)/TPA, Panc-1 (ExP)/TPA, or BxPC-3 (ExBx)/TPA as well as injection of three background foci formed from untreated NIH/3T3 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in all mice injected with Capan-2 exosome/TPA transformed cells at a concentration of 1 × 106 cells.
source: Additional in vivo experiments include subcutaneous injection of mice (n = 5/group) with 1 × 106 cells isolated after treatment with MIA PaCa-2 (ExM)/TPA, Panc-1 (ExP)/TPA, or BxPC-3 (ExBx)/TPA as well as injection of three background foci formed from untreated NIH/3T3 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in all mice injected with MIA PaCa-2 exosome/TPA transformed cells at a concentration of 1 × 106 cells.
source: Additional in vivo experiments include subcutaneous injection of mice (n = 5/group) with 1 × 106 cells isolated after treatment with MIA PaCa-2 (ExM)/TPA, Panc-1 (ExP)/TPA, or BxPC-3 (ExBx)/TPA as well as injection of three background foci formed from untreated NIH/3T3 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in all mice injected with Panc-1 exosome/TPA transformed cells at a concentration of 1 × 106 cells.
source: Additional in vivo experiments include subcutaneous injection of mice (n = 5/group) with 1 × 106 cells isolated after treatment with MIA PaCa-2 (ExM)/TPA, Panc-1 (ExP)/TPA, or BxPC-3 (ExBx)/TPA as well as injection of three background foci formed from untreated NIH/3T3 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Tumor growth was observed in all mice injected with BxPC-3 exosome/TPA transformed cells at a concentration of 1 × 106 cells.
source: Additional in vivo experiments include subcutaneous injection of mice (n = 5/group) with 1 × 106 cells isolated after treatment with MIA PaCa-2 (ExM)/TPA, Panc-1 (ExP)/TPA, or BxPC-3 (ExBx)/TPA as well as injection of three background foci formed from untreated NIH/3T3 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tumor growth data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The tumors formed from transformed cells are fibrosarcomas because cells used in the CTA are NIH/3T3 cells from a mesenchymal origin.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that the tumors are fibrosarcomas, as was expected because cells used in the CTA are NIH/3T3 cells from a mesenchymal origin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the cell type used and confirmed by histological analysis.

claim: Over 1500 proteins were consistently identified in all three replicates of each sample type in the proteomic analysis of transformed cells.
source: In total >1500 proteins were consistently identified in all three replicates of each sample type (see Materials and methods) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cancer cell exosomes and MCA both cause random molecular changes across the population of treated NIH/3T3 cells that cannot be detected amongst the overall protein composition of cells by mass spectrometry.
source: Therefore, potentially both MCA and cancer cell exosomes are causing random molecular changes across the population of treated NIH/3T3 cells that cannot be detected amongst the overall protein composition of cells by mass spectrometry.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for why no major changes were observed in proteomic analysis of initiated cells.

claim: Changes in protein content in initiated cells could not be feasibly detected because they are occurring in specific proteins among specific cells in the total population.
source: Although we observe no major changes in the protein content in initiated cells based on qualitative proteomic analysis, it is logical that changes could not be feasibly detected because they are occurring in specific proteins among specific cells in the total population.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for why no major changes were observed in proteomic analysis of initiated cells.

claim: Each exosome contains a unique repertoire of biological molecules thus possibly causing a variety of changes in the cells.
source: Additionally, it is known that exosomes do not uniformly contain the same pool of proteins, lipids, metabolites, or microRNAs, but rather each exosome contains a unique repertoire of biological molecules thus possibly causing a variety of changes in the cells (Willms et al., 2016; Kowal et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about exosome heterogeneity supported by citations, used to explain why changes might not be detected in bulk analysis.

claim: More studies are needed to elucidate the molecular mechanism of cancer cell exosome-mediated initiation event.
source: Ultimately, more studies are needed to elucidate the molecular mechanism of this cancer cell exosome-mediated initiation event.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the limitations of the current study and the need for future research.

claim: Proteomic studies on transformed cells show major changes in the proteomic profiles compared to control cells.
source: These studies, in contrast to the proteomic studies on the initiator treated cells, show major changes in the proteomic profiles of transformed cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is inferred from the GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4D showing multiple enriched molecular functions in transformed cells.

claim: Each foci was derived from independent mutagenic events.
source: As expected, we observed diversity in mutational variants for each of these pools of cells because each foci was derived from independent mutagenic events (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the mechanism of initiation and supported by the diversity observed in exome sequencing data.

claim: Foci from untreated cells and TPA-only treated samples showed signatures associated with microsatellite instability, but not as the top contributing signature.
source: Foci from untreated cells and TPA-only treated samples did show signatures associated with microsatellite instability, but not as the top contributing signature.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MutaGene analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mismatch repair was found to be the top-contributing signature of each of the transformed foci.
source: Considering that mismatch repair was found to be the top-contributing signature of each of the transformed foci, mismatch repair genes were analyzed in more detail for specific mutations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MutaGene analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The wild-type allele for each MMR gene is still present in the six transformed foci.
source: Concurrently, sequencing data shows that the wild-type allele for each MMR gene is still present in these six foci.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text based on analysis of exome sequencing data.

claim: The presence of the wild-type copy of a MMR gene in somatic cells is not always sufficient for normal function.
source: While MMR genes usually comply with Knudson's two-hit hypothesis for tumor suppressor genes, the presence of the wild-type copy of a MMR gene in somatic cells is not always sufficient for a normal function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MMR gene function.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of MMR genes may be function-specific.
source: Haploinsufficiency may be function-specific; for example, it has been demonstrated that responding to DNA damage requires a higher dosage of MMR protein than the repair function (Peltomäki, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MMR gene function supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The dysfunction of the MMR system is supported by the presence of the COSMIC profiles 20 and 15.
source: Regardless, the dysfunction of the MMR system is supported by the presence of the COSMIC profiles 20 and 15.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MutaGene analysis showing these signatures in transformed foci.

claim: Transformed cells originated from distinct mutagenic events.
source: Interestingly, none of the foci contain the same mutations in the MMR genes, further supporting the proposal that transformed cells originated from distinct mutagenic events.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that each foci has unique mutations in MMR genes.

claim: The main driver found for all six background foci was COSMIC Signature 3, which associates with a failure in DNA double-strand break-repair that compromises genomic integrity.
source: By contrast, only a single sample from the background foci was observed to have mutations (two) in MMR genes. In addition, the main driver found for all six background foci was COSMIC Signature 3. This profile associates with a failure in DNA double-strand break-repair that compromises genomic integrity and likely contributes to the high number of variants found in these samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MutaGene analysis shown in Figure 6 and variant analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: COSMIC Signature 3 likely contributes to the high number of variants found in background foci samples.
source: This profile associates with a failure in DNA double-strand break-repair that compromises genomic integrity and likely contributes to the high number of variants found in these samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known association of COSMIC Signature 3 with genomic instability.

claim: Analysis of the top signatures and perusal of mutated genes for the background foci demonstrates drivers other than MMR genes were used for the transformation of the cells.
source: Analysis of the top signatures and perusal of mutated genes for the background foci demonstrates drivers other than MMR genes were used for the transformation of the cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MutaGene analysis and mutation analysis showing different signatures and mutation patterns in background foci.

claim: Another promoter acting on initiator treated cells might lead cells towards another common endpoint with regards to the 30 different signature profiles.
source: Furthermore, future studies might reveal that another promoter acting on initiator treated cells might lead cells towards another common endpoint with regards to the 30 different signature profiles.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal for future research based on the observation that TPA drives cells towards specific mutational signatures.

claim: Cells in a primary tumor could be derived from exosome-mediated independent transformation events.
source: This elicits a fascinating question as to whether cells in a primary tumor could be derived from independent transformation events as opposed to exclusive clonal events (Felsenstein et al., 2018). Potentially, exosomes secreted by the primary tumor could orchestrate such events.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings that cancer cell exosomes can initiate transformation and the observation from prior literature that some tumors contain genetically unrelated cells.

claim: Additional studies towards understanding the cancer cell exosome-mediated initiation are needed.
source: Additional studies towards understanding the cancer cell exosome-mediated initiation are needed to address such questions, specifically, investigating the initiation capacity of cancer cell exosomes in more relevant cells like human epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging the limitations of the current study and the need for future research.

claim: Investigating the initiation capacity of cancer cell exosomes in more relevant cells like human epithelial cells is needed.
source: Additional studies towards understanding the cancer cell exosome-mediated initiation are needed to address such questions, specifically, investigating the initiation capacity of cancer cell exosomes in more relevant cells like human epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: The classic two-stage CTA was specifically used as a tool to study cell transformation because it is rigorous, reproducible, and has a well-established phenotype.
source: The classic two-stage CTA was specifically used as a tool to study cell transformation because it is rigorous, reproducible, and has a well-established phenotype.
evidence: This is a justification for the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The CTA does not stimulate the entire in vivo neoplastic process, but it can provide essential information about identification of potential carcinogens and their mode of action.
source: This assay does not stimulate the entire in vivo neoplastic process, but it can provide essential information about identification of potential carcinogens and their mode of action.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations and utility of the CTA.

claim: Highly conserved molecular functions exist across human and mouse, including the regulation of cell division, DNA replication, and DNA repair.
source: Previous studies have shown highly conserved molecular functions across human and mouse, including the regulation of cell division, DNA replication, and DNA repair (Monaco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature, used to justify the use of mouse cells with human exosomes.

claim: The two-stage CTA allowed testing of the role that exosomes play in NIH/3T3 cell transformation in a well-controlled manner.
source: Through this assay, we were able to test the role that exosomes play in NIH/3T3 cell transformation in a well-controlled manner.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the experimental approach.

claim: Sustained treatment of NIH/3T3 cells with breast cancer or glioma cell-derived microvesicles has the ability to induce transformation of recipient cells.
source: Interestingly, Antonyak et al. has demonstrated that sustained treatment of NIH/3T3 cells with breast cancer or glioma cell-derived microvesicles has the ability to induce transformation of recipient cells (Antonyak et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from prior literature supported by citation.

claim: When cells were treated only with pancreatic cancer cell exosomes, increased cell transformation was not observed.
source: Contrastingly, in our studies, when cells were treated only with pancreatic cancer cell exosomes, increased cell transformation was not observed.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: Both studies demonstrate that exosomes are indeed playing a role in cell transformation.
source: While the specific details and effects on cell transformation attributed to exosomes vary between the studies, both demonstrate that exosomes are indeed playing a role in cell transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the current study with prior literature.

claim: The initiator activity of cancer cell exosomes is independent of the KRAS mutational state of exosome producing cells.
source: Collectively, we observe that exosomes can function as an initiator in malignant cell transformation. Our results show that this activity is independent of the KRAS mutational state of exosome producing cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing that both KRAS mutant and wild-type cancer cell exosomes can initiate transformation.

claim: Exosomes were found to work as a classic initiator and thus function with multiple promoters (TPA or CdCl2).
source: Additionally, exosomes were found to work as a classic initiator and thus function with multiple promoters (TPA or CdCl2) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Like MCA, cancer cell exosomes can cause random molecular changes to mediate the initiator step in cell transformation.
source: We propose that, like MCA, cancer cell exosomes can cause random molecular changes to mediate the initiator step in cell transformation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations and comparison with MCA.

claim: Treatment with the promoter TPA forces cells to proliferate repeatedly and drives them to be fully transformed.
source: Then, treatment with the promoter TPA forces cells to proliferate repeatedly and drives them to be fully transformed.
evidence: This is a description of the known mechanism of TPA as a promoter in the CTA.

claim: The mutations detected in mismatch repair genes may be deleterious or damaging for the activity of the mismatch repair proteins.
source: Furthermore, based on in silico prediction analysis we observed that the mutations detected in mismatch repair genes may be deleterious or damaging for the activity of the mismatch repair proteins (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in silico prediction analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of MMR genes may occur where responding to DNA damage requires a higher dosage of MMR protein than the repair function.
source: Haploinsufficiency may be function-specific; for example, it has been demonstrated that responding to DNA damage requires a higher dosage of MMR protein than the repair function (Peltomäki, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MMR gene function supported by citation to prior literature.
